documents.text: For twenty-five years, Ananda served as the Buddha's personal attendant, memorizing all his discourses and attending to his every daily need with unmatched devotion.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: Ananda pleaded with the Buddha to allow women to enter the Sangha, leading to the ordination of Mahapajapati Gotami and the establishment of the Bhikkhuni order.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: When Nalagiri, a wild elephant, was set loose to kill the Buddha, Ananda stepped in front of the Buddha to protect him with his own body, ignoring personal safety.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: Ananda went into the monastery, and stood leaning against the lintel of the door, weeping at the thought: "Alas! I remain still but a learner, one who has yet to work out his own perfection. And the Master is about to pass away!"
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: The Blessed One comforted his disciple: "Enough, Ananda! Do not let yourself be troubled; do not weep! Have I not told you that it is in the very nature of things that we must divide ourselves from all things near and dear?"
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: At the First Council, Ananda began every discourse with "Thus have I heard" (Evam me sutam), reciting the Suttas from memory to preserve them for future generations.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: Ananda achieved complete enlightenment (Arhatship) just before the First Buddhist Council opened, earning the praise of all senior monks for his humility, service, and wisdom.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: This entry compiles the historical accounts and translations from T. W. Rhys Davids' "Buddhist Suttas" (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11, 1881), which is in the public domain.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: Arjuna appears in this passage of the Mahabharata under several epithets used by the narrator: "the diadem-decked (Arjuna)", "the ape-bannered Arjuna" (from the emblem of Hanuman on his banner), "Phalguni", "Dhananjaya the son of Pandu", "Vibhatsu", and "the wielder of Gandiva" (his bow), "that chastiser of foes...who was capable of drawing the bow with even his left hand."
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: Krishna, "cheerfully addressing Dhananjaya," told Arjuna: "There, Bhishma, the son of Santanu, stayeth between the two armies. Slaying him by putting forth thy might, thou mayst win victory. There, at that spot, whence he breaketh our ranks, check him, putting forth thy strength." "Thus urged, the ape-bannered Arjuna at that moment made Bhishma with his car, steeds, and standard, invisible by means of his arrows."
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: Because Bhishma had vowed not to raise weapons against a warrior who had formerly been born a woman, Arjuna fought from behind Sikhandin: "Sikhandin, however, that foremost of car-warriors, protected in the battle by the diadem-decked (Arjuna)..." and again, "the diadem-decked (Arjuna), excited with rage and placing Sikhandin to the fore, approached Bhishma (nearer)." The text presents this as a considered battlefield tactic against a vow, not an act the narrator condemns or praises outright — later Mahabharata tradition treats it as morally difficult.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: "Then Vibhatsu, drawing his bow Gandiva with a laugh, pierced the son of Ganga with five and twenty arrows. And once more, Dhananjaya, with great speed and excited with wrath struck him in every vital part with hundreds of arrows...the son of Pandu cut off in that battle even all the bows of Bhishma" — cutting three successive bows from Bhishma's hands with precisely aimed arrows rather than killing him outright.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: Bhishma himself testifies to Arjuna's unmatched skill even while dying from his wounds: "He is incapable of being vanquished in battle by the wielder of the thunder-bolt himself. As regards myself also, O hero, the very gods, Danavas and Rakshasas united together, are incapable of vanquishing me. What I shall say then of mighty car-warriors among men?" — acknowledging Arjuna as the one warrior capable of doing what was done.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: This same Book of the Mahabharata (the Bhishma Parva) also contains the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's counsel to a hesitant Arjuna just before this battle begins, on duty, grief, and right action. The Gita is treated as a separate, already-sourced corpus in this app (the Annie Besant public domain translation) and is not reproduced here; this entry covers only Arjuna's role in the battle narrative that follows it.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: After Bhishma fell, "the heroic Pandavas possessed of massive arms that looked like spiked maces, having obtained the victory and won a highly blessed state in the other world, all blew their great conches." The text records mixed reactions across both armies — grief, shouting, and reflection — rather than simple celebration; Bhishma himself continued to be honored by both sides even after his fall.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: Arjuna (Dhananjaya, Phalguni, Vibhatsu), third of the Pandava brothers, is a central figure of the Mahabharata's Bhishma Parva (Book 6). This entry draws only on Sections CXIX-CXX of the Ganguli translation (1883-1896), public domain, digitized jointly by sacred-texts.com and Project Gutenberg. It does not cover the Bhagavad Gita itself, which is a separate already-sourced corpus, nor other Parvas of the epic.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: "...thy sire Bhishma, influenced by wrath, began to fight with the Srinjayas...the old Kuru grandsire Bhishma, day after day, slew ten thousand warriors of the Ratha. On the tenth day, however...Bhishma, single-handed, slew ten thousand elephants...none of the kings, O monarch, could even look at him, for he then resembled the hot mid-day Sun in the summer sky."
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: Krishna, seeing Bhishma break the Pandava ranks, said to Arjuna: "There, Bhishma, the son of Santanu, stayeth between the two armies. Slaying him by putting forth thy might, thou mayst win victory." Bhishma fought on the Kaurava side out of a prior vow of loyalty to the throne of Hastinapura, not from personal enmity toward the Pandavas, whom the text elsewhere calls his own kin.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: "...he continued...'With only a single bow I could slay all the Pandavas, if the mighty Vishnu himself had not been their protector. For two reasons, however, I will not fight with the Pandavas, viz., their unslayableness, and the femininity of Sikhandin... I should now wish my own death, this being the proper hour.'" Bhishma restrained his own full strength against the Pandavas by choice, even while continuing to fight for the Kaurava army.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: "...he fell down from his car with his head to the east, a little before sunset...That foremost of all bowmen, that mighty-armed hero, fell down, like an uprooted standard of Indra, making the earth tremble the while. Pierced all over with arrows, his body touched not the ground. At that moment...a divine nature took possession of that great bowman lying on a bed of arrows."
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: "The boon that was granted to me by my illustrious sire, to the effect that my death would depend on my own wish O, let that boon become true. I will hold my life, since I have control in the matter of laying it down... I will never pass out (of the world) as long as the Sun is in the southern solstice... I will proceed to my own ancient abode when the Sun reacheth the northern solstice." Bhishma lay on his bed of arrows for many weeks, by his own account, until the turning of the season, so as to die at an auspicious time.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: Of the arrows piercing him, Bhishma told Dussasana: "These arrows coursing towards me in one continuous line, whose touch resembleth that of heaven's bolt, have been shot by Arjuna. These are not Sikhandin's... Save the heroic wielder of Gandiva, viz., the ape-bannered Jishnu, even all other kings united together cannot cause me pain." Even mortally wounded, Bhishma names and honors the skill of the warrior who defeated him rather than complaining of his fate.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: "When the grandsire of the Bharatas who was endued with great might was overthrown, thy son...knew not what to do. And all the Kurus were entirely deprived of their senses... And the Rishis and the Pitris all applauded Bhishma of high vows. And the deceased ancestors of the Bharatas also praised Bhishma." Bhishma, endued with great ascetic merit, "having recourse to that Yoga which is taught in the great Upanishads and engaged in mental prayers, remained quiet, expectant of his hour" even after his fall.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: Bhishma (Devavrata, son of Ganga and Santanu) is a central figure of the Mahabharata's Bhishma Parva (Book 6), which also contains the Bhagavad Gita (a separate, already-sourced corpus in this app). This entry draws only on Sections CXIX-CXX of the Ganguli translation (1883-1896), public domain, digitized jointly by sacred-texts.com and Project Gutenberg. It does not cover Bhishma's earlier vow of lifelong celibacy (Adi Parva, Book 1), which is not yet sourced for this app.
documents.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 6 (Bhishma Parva), translated by Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896)

documents.text: Chanakya (Kautilya) was a teacher at Taxila and counselor to Chandragupta Maurya, seeking to unite the divided kingdoms of India under a single righteous administration.
documents.source_name: Kautilya's Arthashastra, translated by R. Shamasastry (1915)

documents.text: After being insulted by the Nanda king, Chanakya untied his topknot (shikha), vowing to keep it untied until he had destroyed the corrupt dynasty and established a just rule under Chandragupta.
documents.source_name: Kautilya's Arthashastra, translated by R. Shamasastry (1915)

documents.text: Chanakya selected the young Chandragupta, trained him in martial arts and statecraft, and navigated immense political intrigues to guide him to the Maurya throne.
documents.source_name: Kautilya's Arthashastra, translated by R. Shamasastry (1915)

documents.text: Though serving as the prime minister of a vast empire, Chanakya lived in a humble mud hut, stating that a ruler's wealth lies in the prosperity of his subjects, not in personal luxury.
documents.source_name: Kautilya's Arthashastra, translated by R. Shamasastry (1915)

documents.text: "In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness; in their welfare his welfare. What pleases himself he shall not consider as good, but whatever pleases his subjects he shall consider as good." (Rajadharma, Book I, Chapter XIX).
documents.source_name: Kautilya's Arthashastra, translated by R. Shamasastry (1915)

documents.text: "Just as it is impossible not to taste honey or poison that finds itself on the tongue, so it is impossible for a government servant not to eat up at least a bit of the king's revenue," advising strict accountability.
documents.source_name: Kautilya's Arthashastra, translated by R. Shamasastry (1915)

documents.text: Chanakya's guidance led to the creation of the Maurya Empire, which brought peace, unity, and prosperity across the subcontinent, and his writings remain a classic on ethical governance.
documents.source_name: Kautilya's Arthashastra, translated by R. Shamasastry (1915)

documents.text: This entry compiles the translation from R. Shamasastry's "Kautilya's Arthashastra" (1915), which is in the public domain.
documents.source_name: Kautilya's Arthashastra, translated by R. Shamasastry (1915)

documents.text: Dhruva, son of King Uttanapada by his queen Suniti, saw his half-brother Uttama seated on their father's lap and wished to climb up too; but the favourite queen Suruchi, present at the time, rebuked him before the court: ‘Why, child, do you vainly indulge in such presumptuous hopes? You are born from a different mother... This regal throne... is suited to my son only; why should you aspire to its occupation?’
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

documents.text: Dhruva, in tears, ran to his mother Suniti, who, deeply distressed, told him: ‘Suruchi has rightly spoken; thine, child, is an unhappy fate... a wise man will be contented with that degree which appertains to him.’ But Dhruva answered her: ‘Mother, the words that you have addressed to me for my consolation find no place in a heart that contumely has broken. I will exert myself to obtain such elevated rank, that it shall be revered by the whole world... I wish for no other honours than such as my own actions shall acquire, such as even my father has not enjoyed.’
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

documents.text: Dhruva then quitted the city and entered a forest, where he found seven Munis seated on antelope hides. He told them he sought a station no one before him had attained. The sage Marichi said, ‘The best of stations is not within the reach of men who fail to propitiate Govinda. Do thou, prince, worship the undecaying.’ The Rishis taught him the prayer: ‘Om! glory to Vasudeva, whose essence is divine wisdom; whose form is inscrutable, or is manifest as Brahma, Vishnu, and Siva’ — the same prayer, they told him, once uttered by his own grandsire Manu Swayambhuva.
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

documents.text: As Dhruva's mind became wholly absorbed in meditation at Madhuvana on the Yamuna, the earth itself could not sustain the weight of his asceticism, and the gods, alarmed, sent illusions to distract him: an apparition of his weeping mother begging him to desist, then hideous Rakshasas and monsters roaring to terrify him. But 'all these uncouth spectres, appalling cries, and threatening weapons, made no impression upon his senses, whose mind was completely intent on Govinda.'
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

documents.text: Unable to shake him, the gods appealed to Vishnu himself, who at last appeared to the boy in person, four-armed, bearing the shell, discus, mace, bow, and scimetar, and touched him with the tip of his conch-shell. Overwhelmed, Dhruva praised him: ‘I venerate him whose forms are earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect... Salutation to that spirit that is void of qualities... My heart is overflowing with devotion to thee: oh lord, grant me the faculty worthily to lay mine adorations at thy feet.’
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

documents.text: Vishnu asked Dhruva to name his boon, and the boy confessed his original, prideful motive honestly: ‘The sister-queen of my mother has said to me, loudly and arrogantly, “The royal throne is not for one who is not born of me;” and I now solicit of the support of the universe an exalted station, superior to all others, and one that shall endure for ever.’ Vishnu did not rebuke the ambition but granted it: ‘The station that thou askest thou shalt obtain; for I was satisfied with thee of old in a prior existence.’
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

documents.text: Vishnu granted Dhruva a station above the sun, the moon, and all the constellations, to sustain the stars and planets for the duration of a Kalpa, with his mother Suniti abiding near him as a companion star. ‘Wonderful is the efficacy of this penance, marvellous is its reward, that the seven Rishis should be preceded by Dhruva,’ declared Usanas, preceptor of the gods — and to this day Dhruva is identified with the fixed pole star.
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Horace Hayman Wilson's 1840 translation of the Vishnu Purana, Book I, Chapters XI ('Legend of Dhruva') and XII ('Dhruva commences a course of religious austerities'), fetched directly from sacred-texts.com's hosting of this public-domain translation (Wilson died 1860; the translation is unambiguously public domain).
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XI & XII

documents.text: Ashoka inherited the Maurya Empire from his father Bindusara, ruling a vast territory with iron authority before his transformation and dedication to the path of Dharma.
documents.source_name: Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India, by Vincent A. Smith (1901)

documents.text: Directly after the annexation of Kalinga, His Sacred Majesty felt remorse; for the conquest of an unconquered country involves slaughter, death, and captivity of the people, leading Ashoka to embrace Buddhism.
documents.source_name: Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India, by Vincent A. Smith (1901)

documents.text: Ashoka renounced armed conquest (Digvijaya), replacing it with conquest by Dharma (Dharmavijaya), and dedicating imperial resources to public welfare, hospitals, and animal protection.
documents.source_name: Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India, by Vincent A. Smith (1901)

documents.text: Ashoka sent his son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka as Buddhist monastics to spread the message of peace, sacrificing their companionship for the growth of the Sangha.
documents.source_name: Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India, by Vincent A. Smith (1901)

documents.text: The Emperor undertook long pilgrimages to holy sites like Lumbini and Bodh Gaya, replacing royal hunts with tours of piety, and living a disciplined, simple life dedicated to moral uplift.
documents.source_name: Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India, by Vincent A. Smith (1901)

documents.text: "A man must not do reverence to his own sect by disparaging that of another... concord is meritorious, that they should hear and respect each other's Dharma." (Rock Edict XII on tolerance).
documents.source_name: Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India, by Vincent A. Smith (1901)

documents.text: Ashoka's edicts inscribed on pillars and rocks across Asia established a legacy of state-sponsored compassion, religious harmony, and ethical governance that influenced global history.
documents.source_name: Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India, by Vincent A. Smith (1901)

documents.text: This entry compiles the historical translation of the Rock Edicts from Vincent A. Smith's "Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India" (1901), which is in the public domain.
documents.source_name: Asoka, the Buddhist Emperor of India, by Vincent A. Smith (1901)

documents.text: The Kalpa Sutra records that 'the oldest monk of the Venerable Ascetic Mahavira was Indrabhuti of the Gautama gotra, who instructed five hundred Shramanas' -- the senior-most of Mahavira's eleven Ganadharas (chief disciples), among whom two of his own brothers, Agnibhuti and Vayubhuti, also of the Gautama gotra, likewise led five hundred disciples each.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: Of Indrabhuti Gautama and his ten fellow Ganadharas, the text records: 'All these eleven Ganadharas of the Venerable Ascetic Mahavira... knew the twelve Angas, the fourteen Purvas, and the whole Siddhanta of the Ganins' -- complete mastery of Mahavira's teaching, entrusted to them directly by their master.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: Despite being the senior-most and most learned of Mahavira's disciples, Indrabhuti Gautama had not, while his master lived, attained Kevala (omniscience) -- Jacobi's translation records that this was owing to his own deep personal love for Mahavira, an attachment which, however devoted, was itself a bond the tradition holds must finally be cut for liberation.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: On the night that Mahavira died, the Kalpa Sutra records: 'his oldest disciple, the monk Indrabhuti of the Gautama gotra, cut asunder the tie of friendship which he had for his master, and obtained the highest knowledge and intuition, called Kevala, which is infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete, and full.' Only in that moment of profound loss did he attain the omniscience his own attachment had held back.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: Jacobi's note on this episode explains the traditional understanding: 'Being aware that love had no place in one who is free from passion, he suppressed his friendship for his teacher and became a Kevalin' -- a teaching that even the purest devotion to a master, if it remains personal attachment, is itself among the last bonds to be released on the path to liberation.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: In the account of Mahavira's final community, the Kalpa Sutra records 'an excellent community of fourteen thousand Shramanas with Indrabhuti at their head' -- naming Gautama as literally the head of Mahavira's entire monastic order among the tens of thousands of monks, nuns, and lay followers left behind.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: Gautama lived twelve years after Mahavira's death, dying at ninety-two after fifty years as a monk. Yet the Kalpa Sutra notes that it was not through Gautama but through his younger colleague, Arya Sudharman, that the continuing line of teachers passed down to later generations: 'The Nirgrantha Shramanas of the present time are all (spiritual) descendants of the monk Arya Sudharman, the rest of the Ganadharas left no descendants' -- Gautama's own line, despite his seniority and devotion, was not the one the tradition continued through.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Hermann Jacobi's 1884 translation of the Kalpa Sutra (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22) -- the 'Life of Mahavira' (Lecture 5) and the 'List of the Sthaviras' -- fetched directly from the sacred-texts.com etext. The source refers to this figure throughout by his personal name, Indrabhuti, of the Gautama gotra; he is popularly known today as Gautama Swami.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: Bibi Bhani, wife of Guru Ram Das, gave birth to Arjan at Goindwal on Tuesday the 7th day of the dark half of Baisakh, Sambat 1620 (A.D. 1563). His grandfather Guru Amar Das foretold of the child, "this grandson of mine shall be a boat to take mankind across the ocean of the world."
documents.source_name: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. III (1909)

documents.text: After Guru Ram Das's death, Arjan's elder brother Prithia contested the succession and complained to Mughal officials and to the chaudhris of Amritsar that he had been left without maintenance. Rather than contest it, Guru Arjan granted certain taxes and house rents to Prithia and the customs duties of a ward of Amritsar to his second brother Mahadev, reserving for himself only the voluntary offerings of the faithful.
documents.source_name: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. III (1909)

documents.text: Guru Arjan applied himself to completing the tanks of Santokhsar and Amritsar begun under his father, and projected the Har Mandar, the temple of God at their centre. He appointed his most trustworthy Sikhs -- Bhais Budha, Salo, Bhagtu, Paira, Bahlo, Kaliana and others -- to superintend the work and procure lime, bricks, and all other necessary materials.
documents.source_name: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. III (1909)

documents.text: When a Jogi found beneath the site of the Santokhsar tank asked who now reigned and how the world had changed, Guru Arjan answered with a hymn on impermanence: "A player playeth his part, and representeth many characters; but when he taketh off his disguises the play is brought to an end, and he assumeth his original appearance... Man goeth astray through the sins of covetousness and worldly love; but, when he is freed from his error, he assumeth the likeness of God, who is imperishable and perisheth not."
documents.source_name: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. III (1909)

documents.text: Sent to the hill state of Mandi to raise funds, the Sikh Bhai Kaliana alone refused the Raja's order that all fast and worship the salagram stone on Krishna's birth anniversary. Confronted by the angered Raja, he declared, "My God is a living Being who speaketh and conferreth great happiness on His worshippers. Vain is the worship of a lifeless stone which neither eateth, nor speaketh, nor conferreth favours," and recited Guru Arjan's hymn: "God is not subject to birth and death... Nanak's God is everywhere; He is not born, nor doth He die; He cometh not and goeth not."
documents.source_name: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. III (1909)

documents.text: To further the completion of the Amritsar tank and the collection of sacred texts, Guru Arjan sent his Sikh Paira on a difficult journey to the King of Ceylon to obtain the Pransangali, a religious text, for the Guru's library -- an episode the tradition preserves as an example of the Guru's determination to gather every genuine source of scripture and knowledge available to his Sikhs.
documents.source_name: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. III (1909)

documents.text: Guru Arjan resolved to compile the exact words of the Gurus into one grand volume, both to give his followers consistent guidance and to counter his brother Prithia, who was composing his own hymns and passing them off as the compositions of Guru Nanak and his successors to an ignorant populace unable to tell the difference. He sent Gur Das and then Bhai Budha to Goindwal to obtain the volumes of the Gurus' compositions kept by Mohan, the elder son of the third Guru -- the opening act of what would become the compilation of the Adi Granth.
documents.source_name: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. III (1909)

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Max Arthur Macauliffe's The Sikh Religion, Vol. III (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909), a public-domain work, as fetched directly from the archive.org full-text scan of the Digital Library of India copy (identifier in.ernet.dli.2015.69684, dc.rights: Out_of_copyright). It covers the Guru's birth, succession, the founding of the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple), and the beginning of the Adi Granth's compilation (Chapters I and VII, pp. 1-56). The Guru's 1606 martyrdom, recounted later in the same volume, is not yet represented in this corpus pending direct source verification.
documents.source_name: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. III (1909)

documents.text: "The Guru, on seeing his son, felt his end was near, and having placed the coconut and five paisa before him, bowed to him in token of his succession." Born in Patna, Gobind Rai succeeded his father Guru Tegh Bahadur at a young age to lead the Sikhs.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 5, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: "The Guru arose and said: 'Is there any Sikh of mine who will offer his head to my sword?' ... When five Sikhs had thus offered their lives, he baptized them with Amrit (holy nectar) and declared them the Panj Pyare (the Five Beloved Ones), initiating the Khalsa in 1699."
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 5, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: The Guru's family and disciples faced extreme hunger and cold during the prolonged siege of Anandpur. Yet the Guru refused to surrender, reminding them that the path of Dharma requires enduring all trials.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 5, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, the Guru's eldest sons, fell fighting bravely against overwhelming forces at Chamkaur. The Guru watched them go to battle with joy, stating: "O God, it is You who gave them to me, and I return them to You in battle for Dharma."
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 5, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: The two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were bricked up alive at Sirhind for refusing to renounce their faith. They stated: "Our grandfather Guru Tegh Bahadur gave his life but not his faith; we shall follow his path."
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 5, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: "When all other means have failed, it is righteous to draw the sword." In his letter (Zafarnama) to Aurangzeb, the Guru declared that he did not fear imperial armies, for his trust was in the Lord of the universe.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 5, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Before passing, the Guru placed the coconut and five paisa before the Adi Granth, bowed, and said: "Let him who desires to behold me look into the Granth Sahib. Obey the Granth Sahib as the visible body of the Gurus."
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 5, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: This entry compiles the historical accounts and translations from Max Arthur Macauliffe's "The Sikh Religion", Vol. 5 (1909), which is in the public domain and hosted on sacred-texts.com.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 5, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Born in Talwandi, Guru Nanak from his childhood was of a contemplative mind, preferring spiritual discussions to trade or agriculture, and refusing to wear the ritual thread, seeking instead the inner thread of love and truth.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: After emerging from three days in the Bein River, Guru Nanak declared: "There is no Hindu, and there is no Musalman," asserting the unity of humanity under one Creator and initiating his mission.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Guru Nanak walked thousands of miles across India, Mecca, and Tibet (in journeys known as Udasis), facing hostile crowds, wild beasts, and imprisonment to spread the message of truth and devotion.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Confronting the robber Sajjan, who murdered travelers, the Guru sang a hymn about deceitful lives, causing Sajjan to repent, give up his wealth, and build the first dharamsala (house of worship).
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Imprisoned by Babur's invading army, Guru Nanak's spiritual poise impressed the Emperor, who released the prisoners and sought the Guru's blessing, recognizing his divine authority.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Guru Nanak established the three pillars of Sikh life: earn an honest living (Kirat Karo), remember the Divine Name (Naam Japna), and share your earnings with the needy (Vand Chhako).
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Establishing a community of farmers at Kartarpur where all dined together in a common kitchen (Langar), the Guru chose his devoted disciple Bhai Lehna (Guru Angad) as his successor, passing his light to him.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: This entry compiles the historical accounts and translations from Max Arthur Macauliffe's "The Sikh Religion", Vol. 1 (1909), which is in the public domain and hosted on sacred-texts.com.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Tegh Bahadur spent twenty years in quiet contemplation in a cellar at Bakala, until he was revealed to the public by Makhan Shah Lubana who cried, "Guru Ladho re" (The Guru has been found), acknowledging his spiritual path.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 4, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: When Kashmiri Pandits sought the Guru's protection from forced conversion, the Guru told them: "Tell the Emperor that if he converts Guru Tegh Bahadur, you will all follow him," defending their freedom of religion.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 4, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Knowing the certainty of death, the Guru traveled to Delhi to meet the Emperor, offering himself as a sacrifice to protect the liberty of conscience of another faith.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 4, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: The Guru's close disciples Bhai Mati Das (sawn alive), Bhai Sati Das (burnt alive), and Bhai Dayala (boiled in water) were executed before him, yet they all died with the Guru's hymns on their lips.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 4, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Refusing to show a miracle or convert, the Guru was beheaded in Delhi in 1675, showing that life is fleeting but truth and honor are eternal.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 4, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: In his hymns of detachment (Salok Mahalla 9), the Guru taught: "Fear not, nor frighten anyone" (Bhai Kahu Kau Det Neh, Neh Bhai Manat Aan), as the key to spiritual liberation.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 4, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: The sacrifice of Guru Tegh Bahadur galvanized the Sikh community, leading his son Guru Gobind Singh to establish the Khalsa to fight oppression and secure human rights.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 4, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: This entry compiles the historical accounts and translations from Max Arthur Macauliffe's "The Sikh Religion", Vol. 4 (1909), which is in the public domain and hosted on sacred-texts.com.
documents.source_name: The Sikh Religion, Vol. 4, translated by Max Arthur Macauliffe (1909)

documents.text: Charged by the Vanar army to find Sita, held captive across the sea in Ravana's Lanka, Hanuman alone resolved to make the leap no other could attempt. Standing on the mountain's height before his kinsmen, he vowed: 'Swift as a shaft from Rama's bow to Ravan's city will I go, and if she be not there will fly and seek the lady in the sky; or, if in heaven she be not found, will hither bring the giant bound.'
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

documents.text: Hanuman sprang from the mountain crest across the ocean toward Lanka, his shadow flying over the sea 'like a ship before the gale.' The mountain Mainaka, moved by gratitude to Rama's line, rose from the sea to offer him rest — but Hanuman, single-minded in his mission, would not pause: 'I may not rest, the Vanar cried; I must not stay or turn aside. Yet pleased am I, thou noblest hill, and as the deed accept thy will.'
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

documents.text: The serpent-mother Surasa barred his path in monstrous form, declaring him her destined prey by Brahma's decree, and opened her jaws impossibly wide to swallow him. Hanuman matched her, growing his own form ever larger, then in an instant shrank himself smaller than a thumb, darted through her mouth, and emerged unharmed on the other side — defeating her by wit rather than force, and she blessed his onward journey.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

documents.text: Next the demoness Sinhika seized his shadow from the deep and opened her jaws to devour him. Hanuman shrank his body, leapt inside her gaping mouth, tore through her from within, and burst out again 'with thought-like speed,' slaying her outright — a feat the watching spirits hailed from the sky: 'Well hast thou fought a wondrous fight... Ne're can they fail in whom combine such valour, thought, and skill as thine.'
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

documents.text: Having reduced himself to the size of a cat to search unseen, Hanuman entered Ravana's pleasure gardens and at last found the Ashoka grove, reasoning that a grieving queen would be drawn to its cool, lovely shade: 'Here the sad queen will roam apart, and dream of Rama in her heart' — the quiet, careful searching of a devoted servant, patient even after crossing an ocean and battling monsters to get there.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

documents.text: Hanuman's entire mission across this batch's chunks illustrates a single, sustained quality: total devotion to Rama's purpose that neither honour (Mainaka's offered rest), nor threat (Surasa), nor mortal danger (Sinhika) could turn aside from its object — reasoning always by resourcefulness rather than force alone when force would not serve.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

documents.text: Hanuman's leap across the ocean to Lanka, and his subsequent discovery of Sita in the Ashoka grove, is the turning point of the Ramayana's Sundara Kanda (Book V) — the moment that confirms Sita is alive and locatable, and sets in motion the war that will free her. Tradition venerates Hanuman above all as the ideal of selfless, resourceful service (dasya bhakti) to Rama.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Ralph T. H. Griffith's verse translation of the Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889, unambiguously public domain), Book V, Chapters I ('Hanuman's Leap') and XIV ('The Ashoka Grove'), fetched directly from wisdomlib.org's hosting of this public-domain translation. Later chapters covering Hanuman's meeting with Sita, the burning of Lanka, and his role in the war were not directly fetched/verified in this batch.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book V

documents.text: Harishchandra ruled Ayodhya with justice and piety, having vowed that he would never speak a lie under any circumstances, gaining reknown for his truthfulness.
documents.source_name: The Markandeya Purana, translated by F. Eden Pargiter (1904)

documents.text: To fulfill a promise made in a dream and tested by Sage Vishvamitra, Harishchandra gladly gave away his kingdom, wealth, and empire, walking out as a pauper to preserve his integrity.
documents.source_name: The Markandeya Purana, translated by F. Eden Pargiter (1904)

documents.text: To pay the ritual fee (dakshina) demanded by the sage, Harishchandra sold his wife Shaivya and young son Rohitashva into slavery to a brahmin, bearing the pain of separation.
documents.source_name: The Markandeya Purana, translated by F. Eden Pargiter (1904)

documents.text: To pay the remaining fee, the King sold himself to an outcaste who managed the cremation grounds, performing the menial duty of collecting shroud-fees from the dead.
documents.source_name: The Markandeya Purana, translated by F. Eden Pargiter (1904)

documents.text: When his son died of a snakebite and Shaivya brought the body for cremation, Harishchandra refused to burn the body without the standard fee, prioritizing his duty and truth over personal grief.
documents.source_name: The Markandeya Purana, translated by F. Eden Pargiter (1904)

documents.text: Harishchandra taught that Dharma is rooted in Truth. A kingdom may fall and life may perish, but Truth must never be abandoned under any pressure or trial.
documents.source_name: The Markandeya Purana, translated by F. Eden Pargiter (1904)

documents.text: Impressed by his absolute integrity, the gods appeared, restored his son to life, and invited Harishchandra and his loyal subjects to ascend to the heavens in glory.
documents.source_name: The Markandeya Purana, translated by F. Eden Pargiter (1904)

documents.text: This entry compiles the translation from F. Eden Pargiter's "The Markandeya Purana" (1904), published by the Asiatic Society of Bengal, which is in the public domain.
documents.source_name: The Markandeya Purana, translated by F. Eden Pargiter (1904)

documents.text: Underhill records that Kabir was 'born in or near Benares, of Mohammedan parents, and probably about the year 1440,' most likely as the son of a Mohammedan weaver of that city. He never adopted the life of the professional ascetic: 'all the legends agree on this point: that Kabir was a weaver, a simple and unlettered man, who earned his living at the loom... he was no ascetic, but a married man, the father of a family... it was from out of the heart of the common life that he sang his rapturous lyrics of divine love.'
documents.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

documents.text: Tradition holds that the boy Kabir, of Muslim birth, knew a Hindu guru would be unlikely to accept him as a disciple, and so hid on the steps of the Ganges where the celebrated ascetic Ramananda bathed each morning. When Ramananda came down to the water he trod on Kabir's body unexpectedly and exclaimed in astonishment, 'Ram! Ram!' -- the name of his own God. Kabir then declared he had received the mantra of initiation from Ramananda's own lips, and in spite of the protests of orthodox Brahmans and Mohammedans alike, persisted in his claim to discipleship, exhibiting in action the very principle of religious synthesis Ramananda had sought to establish in thought.
documents.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

documents.text: Kabir denounced empty ritual, whether Hindu or Muslim, as no substitute for direct communion with God: 'The images are all lifeless, they cannot speak: I know, for I have cried aloud to them. The Purana and the Koran are mere words: lifting up the curtain, I have seen.' He taught that God was 'neither in Kaaba nor in Kailash' and that those who sought Him needed not go far, for He was more accessible to 'the washerwoman and the carpenter' than to the self-righteous holy man.
documents.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

documents.text: Refusing to be claimed by either creed, Kabir said of himself that he was 'at once the child of Allah and of Ram.' He poured contempt on professional sanctity, on the Yogi who 'has a great beard and matted locks, and looks like a goat,' and on all who thought it necessary to flee the world in search of the One Reality who has 'spread His form of love throughout all the world' -- teaching that home and daily life, not the ascetic's cell, were the proper theatre of the soul's love and renunciation.
documents.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

documents.text: Kabir's rejection of institutional religion made him, in Underhill's words, 'plainly a heretic' in the eyes of both orthodox Hindus and Mohammedans, and he 'was subjected to considerable persecution' with his headquarters in Benares, the very center of priestly influence. He was at least once brought before the Emperor Sikandar Lodi and charged with claiming divine powers after performing a supposed miracle of healing; though his life was spared, he was banished from Benares in the interests of peace around 1495, when he was nearly sixty years of age.
documents.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

documents.text: Exiled from Benares, Kabir moved among the cities of northern India as the center of a group of disciples, 'continuing in exile that life of apostle and poet of love to which, as he declares in one of his songs, he was destined "from the beginning of time."' In 1518, an old man broken in health, with hands too feeble to make the music he loved, he died at Maghar near Gorakhpur.
documents.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

documents.text: A legend recorded by Underhill tells that after Kabir's death, his Mohammedan and Hindu disciples disputed over his body -- the Mohammedans wishing to bury it, the Hindus to burn it. As they argued, Kabir himself appeared and told them to lift the shroud and look beneath. They found, in the place of the corpse, a heap of flowers; half were buried by the Mohammedans at Maghar, half carried by the Hindus to Benares to be burned -- 'fitting conclusion to a life which had made fragrant the most beautiful doctrines of two great creeds.'
documents.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Evelyn Underhill's biographical Introduction to Rabindranath Tagore's 1915 translation 'Songs of Kabir' (New York: The Macmillan Company), fetched directly from the sacred-texts.com etext, which states it 'is in the public domain in the US because it was published prior to 1923.' Underhill explicitly flags Kabir's traditional biography as legendary and not reliably attested; this manifest preserves that framing. The translated songs themselves (the poems proper) were not fetched in this batch; only the biographical Introduction was used.
documents.source_name: Songs of Kabir, translated by Rabindranath Tagore, Introduction by Evelyn Underhill (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1915)

documents.text: "...the Venerable Ascetic Mahavira, the last of the Tirthakaras...took the form of an embryo in the womb of Devananda...in the brahmanical part of the town Kundagrama." By the god Sakra's order, the embryo was then transferred to the womb of "the Kshatriyani Trisala...wife of the Kshatriya Siddhartha," since it is held that Arhats are never born from a brahmanical womb, only a noble Kshatriya one.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira

documents.text: "The Venerable Ascetic Mahavira belonged to the Kasyapa gotra. His three names have thus been recorded: by his parents he was called Vardhamana; because he is devoid of love and hate, he is called Sramana (i.e. Ascetic); because he stands fast in midst of dangers and fears, patiently bears hardships and calamities, adheres to the chosen rules of penance, is wise, indifferent to pleasure and pain, rich in control, and gifted with fortitude, the name Venerable Ascetic Mahavira has been given him by the gods."
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira

documents.text: At age thirty, after his parents' death, Mahavira renounced the world: "He left his silver, he left his gold, he left his riches, corn, majesty, and kingdom...he distributed presents through proper persons, he distributed presents among indigent persons." He then "descended from his palankin, took off his ornaments, garlands, and finery with his own hands, and with his own hands plucked out his hair in five handfuls," fasting two and a half days before entering "the state of houselessness."
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira

documents.text: "The Venerable Ascetic Mahavira for a year and a month wore clothes; after that time he walked about naked, and accepted the alms in the hollow of his hand. For more than twelve years the Venerable Ascetic Mahavira neglected his body and abandoned the care of it; he with equanimity bore, underwent, and suffered all pleasant or unpleasant occurrences arising from divine powers, men, or animals."
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira

documents.text: Of his equanimity through those years of austerity: "his heart was pure like the water...in autumn; nothing could soil him like the leaf of a lotus; his senses were well protected like those of a tortoise; he was single and alone like the horn of a rhinoceros; he was free like a bird...strong like a bull, difficult to attack like a lion, steady and firm like Mount Mandara, deep like the ocean, mild like the moon...pure like excellent gold...like a well-kindled fire he shone in his splendour."
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira

documents.text: After thirteen years of ascetic practice, "outside of the town Grimbhikagrama on the bank of the river Rigupalika...under a Sal tree...in a squatting position with joined heels, exposing himself to the heat of the sun, after fasting two and a half days without drinking water, being engaged in deep meditation, (he) reached the highest knowledge and intuition, called Kevala, which is infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete, and full." As a Kevalin, the text says he then "knew and saw all conditions of the world."
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira

documents.text: Mahavira taught for thirty more years before dying at Pava. The text records his community at the time of his death as "an excellent community of fourteen thousand Sramanas...thirty-six thousand nuns...one hundred and fifty-nine thousand lay votaries...three hundred and eighteen thousand female lay votaries," among other named ranks of advanced disciples — the fourfold Jain community (monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen) that continues today.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira

documents.text: Mahavira (Vardhamana), the 24th and last Tirthakara of this era in Jain tradition, is the subject of the Kalpa Sutra's Life of Mahavira (Lectures 1-5). This entry draws only on Lecture 2 (conception) and Lecture 5 (naming, renunciation, austerities, enlightenment, death, community) of Hermann Jacobi's 1884 translation, Sacred Books of the East vol. 22, public domain. The Kalpa Sutra's earlier lectures and its separate Life of Parsva are not reproduced here.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira

documents.text: Partap succeeded to the titles and renown of an illustrious house, but without a capital, without resources, his kindred and clans dispirited by reverses. Yet possessed of the noble spirit of his race, he meditated the recovery of Chitor and the restoration of Mewar's power, even as the Mogul arrayed against him princes of his own faith and blood -- Marwar, Amber, Bikaner, and even his own brother Sagarji, who deserted him for the price of Chitor's title.
documents.source_name: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, Book IV Ch. 11

documents.text: To commemorate the desolation of Chitor, Partap interdicted to himself and his successors every article of luxury or pomp until Chitor's honour should be redeemed: gold and silver dishes were laid aside for leaf-plates, beds of straw replaced beds of comfort, and beards were left untouched. He commanded that the martial drums, which always led the van in battle or procession, should follow in the rear instead -- a sign of Mewar's fallen fortune that survived among his descendants long after.
documents.source_name: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, Book IV Ch. 11

documents.text: When Raja Man Singh of Amber, whose family had married into the Mughal court, visited Partap at Kumbhalmer, Partap refused to dine with him, sending word: "he could not eat with a Rajput who gave his sister to a Turk." Raja Man Singh withdrew in fury, vowing "If I do not humble your pride, my name is not Man" -- an insult to Akbar's court that helped precipitate the war culminating at Haldighat.
documents.source_name: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, Book IV Ch. 11

documents.text: At the Battle of Haldighat (18 June 1576), Partap led the crimson banner into the hottest part of the field, his steed Chetak rearing with one foot upon the Mogul elephant as the prince's lance was leveled at Prince Salim. Marked by the royal umbrella he would not lay aside, Partap was thrice rescued and nearly overwhelmed when the Jhala chief Mana seized the insignia of Mewar and drew the enemy upon himself, giving his life so that Partap could be forced from the field. Of twenty-two thousand Rajputs who fought that day, only eight thousand left the field alive.
documents.source_name: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, Book IV Ch. 11

documents.text: Fleeing alone on the wounded Chetak, Partap was closely pursued by two Mogul horsemen until a lone rider called out in his native tongue, "Ho! rider of the blue horse" -- his estranged brother Sakta, who had fought for Akbar but now turned to slay the pursuers. Chetak died of his wounds at that spot; the brothers embraced for the first time in their lives, and Sakta was pardoned by Prince Salim on the promise that he had only defended his brother, "The burthen of a kingdom is on my brother's shoulders, nor could I witness his danger without defending him from it."
documents.source_name: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, Book IV Ch. 11

documents.text: During the years of guerrilla resistance that followed, Partap's family was repeatedly in danger of capture; on one occasion the faithful Bhils of Kava carried them in wicker baskets and hid them in the tin mines of Jawara. In one privation, his daughter's cry from hunger -- as a wild cat snatched the last reserved portion of grass-flour cake from the family -- was, in the chronicler's words, the one thing that "unmanned" Partap after he had watched his sons fall in battle without emotion, "for this the Rajput was born."
documents.source_name: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, Book IV Ch. 11

documents.text: Partap's minister Bhama Shah placed at the prince's disposal his family's accumulated wealth -- said to be enough to maintain twenty-five thousand men for twelve years -- enabling Partap to surprise the Mogul garrisons and recover Kumbhalmer, Udaipur, and nearly all of Mewar except Chitor itself. On his deathbed, Partap made his chiefs swear "by the throne of Bappa Rawal" that they would not build sumptuous dwellings until Mewar had recovered her full independence. Tod's annals close the chapter: "Haldighat is the Thermopylae of Mewar; the field of Dawer her Marathon."
documents.source_name: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, Book IV Ch. 11

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from James Tod's Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan (1829), Book IV, Chapter 11, 'Rana Partap Singh, A.D. 1572-97', as transcribed in William Crooke's 1920 annotated edition and hosted by the ibiblio.org 'British Raj' public-domain text collection. Tod's work is unambiguously public domain (author died 1835); the ibiblio.org transcription is presented for non-commercial educational and research use.
documents.source_name: James Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan, Book IV Ch. 11

documents.text: King Milinda went up to where the venerable Nagasena was, and addressed him with the greetings and compliments of friendship and courtesy, and took his seat respectfully apart. And Milinda began by asking, ‘How is your Reverence known, and what, Sir, is your name?’ Nagasena replied that his brethren addressed him as Nagasena, but that this, like Surasena or Virasena, was only a generally understood term, a designation in common use — ‘for there is no permanent individuality (no soul) involved in the matter.’
documents.source_name: T. W. Rhys Davids (trans.), The Questions of King Milinda, Sacred Books of the East Vol. 35 (1890), Book II Chapter 1

documents.text: Milinda called upon the Yonakas and the brethren to witness: ‘This Nagasena says there is no permanent individuality (no soul) implied in his name. Is it now even possible to approve him in that?’ He pressed Nagasena hard: if there is no soul, who is it who gives alms, who lives righteously, who destroys life or speaks lies? ‘If that be so there is neither merit nor demerit... It is a falsehood that your reverence has spoken, an untruth!’ And the five hundred Yonakas shouted their applause.
documents.source_name: T. W. Rhys Davids (trans.), The Questions of King Milinda, Sacred Books of the East Vol. 35 (1890), Book II Chapter 1

documents.text: Nagasena asked the king whether he had come on foot or by chariot, and then asked him to explain what the chariot was — was it the pole, the wheels, the framework, the ropes, the yoke? To each Milinda answered no, yet insisted a chariot existed. Nagasena replied: ‘Just even so it is on account of all those things you questioned me about— the thirty-two kinds of organic matter in a human body, and the five constituent elements of being—that I come under the generally understood term, the designation in common use, of “Nagasena.” ... Just as it is by the condition precedent of the co-existence of its various parts that the word ‘chariot’ is used, just so is it that when the Skandhas are there we talk of a ‘being.’’ Milinda exclaimed: ‘Most wonderful, Nagasena, and most strange. Well has the puzzle put to you, most difficult though it was, been solved. Were the Buddha himself here he would approve your answer.’
documents.source_name: T. W. Rhys Davids (trans.), The Questions of King Milinda, Sacred Books of the East Vol. 35 (1890), Book II Chapter 1

documents.text: The king asked whether Nagasena would discuss with him again, and Nagasena answered: ‘If your Majesty will discuss as a scholar, well; but if you will discuss as a king, no... When a king discusses a matter, and he advances a point, if any one differ from him on that point, he is apt to fine him, saying: “Inflict such and such a punishment upon that fellow!”’ Milinda accepted the correction: ‘It is as a scholar, not as a king, that I will discuss. Let your reverence talk unrestrainedly, as you would with a brother, or a novice, or a lay disciple, or even with a servant. Be not afraid!’ — setting aside his royal power to submit to honest philosophical argument.
documents.source_name: T. W. Rhys Davids (trans.), The Questions of King Milinda, Sacred Books of the East Vol. 35 (1890), Book II Chapter 1

documents.text: The king asked Nagasena: ‘What is the object, Sir, of your renunciation, and what the summum bonum at which you aim?’ Nagasena replied: ‘Our renunciation is to the end that this sorrow may perish away, and that no further sorrow may arise; the complete passing away, without cleaving to the world, is our highest aim.’ Milinda then asked whether all members of the Order had joined for such high reasons, and Nagasena answered honestly: ‘Certainly not, Sire. Some for those reasons, but some have left the world in terror at the tyranny of kings. Some have joined us to be safe from being robbed, some harassed by debt, and some perhaps to gain a livelihood.’
documents.source_name: T. W. Rhys Davids (trans.), The Questions of King Milinda, Sacred Books of the East Vol. 35 (1890), Book II Chapter 1

documents.text: Testing Nagasena further, Milinda asked how many years' seniority he had. ‘Seven, your Majesty.’ ‘Is it you who are “seven,” or the number that is “seven?”’ Nagasena pointed to the king's own shadow cast upon the ground and reflected in water, and asked whether the king was the shadow. ‘I am the king, Nagasena, but the shadow comes into existence because of me.’ ‘Just even so, O king, the number of the years is seven, I am not seven. But it is because of me... that the number seven has come into existence.’ Milinda again conceded: ‘Most wonderful again, and strange, Nagasena.’
documents.source_name: T. W. Rhys Davids (trans.), The Questions of King Milinda, Sacred Books of the East Vol. 35 (1890), Book II Chapter 1

documents.text: Having grasped that scholars discuss by ‘winding up’ and ‘unravelling’ an argument until one acknowledges his mistake, without anger, Milinda set aside the discussion until the following day, and had food, garments, and a set of three robes prepared for Nagasena and ten of his brethren. He then took a lower seat beside his teacher and said, ‘What shall we discuss?’, to which Nagasena replied, ‘We want to arrive at truth. Let our discussion be about the truth’ — setting the terms on which the whole dialogue that follows in the Milinda Panha is conducted.
documents.source_name: T. W. Rhys Davids (trans.), The Questions of King Milinda, Sacred Books of the East Vol. 35 (1890), Book II Chapter 1

documents.text: The Arhat Parsva was born in Varanasi as the son of King Asvasena and Queen Vama, living 250 years before the nirvana of Mahavira as a prince of noble character.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Parsva

documents.text: Parsva renounced his royal life to establish the four great vows (Chaturyama Dharma): non-violence (ahimsa), truthfulness (satya), non-stealing (asteya), and non-possession (aparigraha).
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Parsva

documents.text: While Parsva sat in deep meditation, the demon Kamatha (his enemy from past lives) raised a terrifying storm, hurling rain, winds, and stones to break his spiritual resolve.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Parsva

documents.text: The serpent king Dharanendra rose from the earth and spread his seven hoods over Parsva's head like an umbrella, protecting him from the fury of the storm.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Parsva

documents.text: Throughout the storm and the protection, Parsva remained completely detached, feeling neither anger towards the demon nor attachment to the protector, maintaining perfect equanimity.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Parsva

documents.text: Parsva taught that all souls are equal and that the highest spiritual duty is the absolute avoidance of harm to any living being, visible or invisible, establishing the foundation of Jain ethics.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Parsva

documents.text: After seventy years of teaching, Parsva achieved ultimate liberation (Nirvana) on Mount Sammed Shikhar, which remains today the most sacred pilgrimage site for Jains.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), translated by Hermann Jacobi (1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Parsva

documents.text: This entry compiles the translation from Hermann Jacobi's "Jaina Sutras, Part I" (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22, 1884), Kalpa Sutra: Life of Parsva, which is in the public domain.

documents.text: Prahlada, the illustrious son of the Daitya king Hiranyakasipu, resided as a boy in the dwelling of his preceptor, where he read such writings as are studied in early years. Brought before his father and asked to repeat what he had learned, Prahlada answered: ‘I have learned to adore him who is without beginning, middle, or end, increase or diminution; the imperishable lord of the world, the universal cause of causes.’ When his father demanded who had taught him this, Prahlada replied, ‘Vishnu, father, is the instructor of the whole world: what else should any one teach or learn, save him the supreme spirit?’
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

documents.text: Enraged, Hiranyakasipu cried ‘Kill the wretch! he is not fit to live,’ and his attendants rushed upon Prahlada with weapons. The prince calmly said: ‘Daityas, as truly as Vishnu is present in your weapons and in my body, so truly shall those weapons fail to harm me’; and though struck heavily and repeatedly by hundreds of the Daityas, Prahlada felt not the least pain, and his strength was ever renewed.
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

documents.text: Hiranyakasipu next commanded the great snakes Kuhaka, Takshaka, and Andhaka to bite his son with their envenomed fangs; but Prahlada, his thoughts immovably fixed on Krishna, felt no pain, and the snakes cried out to the king, ‘Our fangs are broken... but the skin of the youth is still unscathed.’ Then elephants of the skies were sent to gore and trample him, but their tusks were blunted against his breast; Prahlada said, ‘Calling upon Janarddana is my defence against such fearful affliction.’
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

documents.text: The king then ordered a mighty heap of wood piled around the prince and set alight. But Prahlada cried, ‘Father, this fire, though blown up by the winds, burneth me not; and all around I behold the face of the skies, cool and fragrant, with beds of lotus flowers.’ Priests who witnessed this pleaded with Hiranyakasipu to restrain his wrath against his own son, and the prince was liberated from the flames.
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

documents.text: Returned to his preceptor's house, Prahlada gave lessons to the sons of the demons in the intervals of his leisure: ‘Sons of the offspring of Diti, hear from me the supreme truth... Birth, infancy, and youth are the portion of all creatures; and then succeeds gradual and inevitable decay... Verily I say unto you, that in this ocean of the world, this sea of many sorrows, Vishnu is your only hope... Let all your thoughts and affections be fixed on him, who is present in all beings, and you shall laugh at every care.’
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

documents.text: Meditating upon Vishnu as identical with his own spirit, Prahlada became as one with him, and in consequence the bonds with which he was bound burst instantly asunder; the ocean was violently uplifted, and the prince, putting aside the rocks the demons had piled upon him, came forth from out the main. He hymned Purushottama: ‘Om! glory to the end of all: to thee, lord, who art subtile and substantial; mutable and immutable; perceptible and imperceptible... Oh thou who art both one and many, Vasudeva, first cause of all; glory be unto thee.’
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

documents.text: When Vishnu appeared before him and offered a boon, Prahlada asked not for his own sake but for his father's: ‘I have been hated, for that I assiduously proclaimed thy praise: do thou, oh lord, pardon in my father this sin that he hath committed... do thou therefore free my father from this iniquity.’ After Hiranyakasipu was slain by Vishnu in the form of the man-lion (Narasimha), Prahlada became the sovereign of the Daityas, ruling with the splendours of piety, and the text promises that whoever hears his history is cleansed from sin.
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book I Chapters XVII & XX

Chapters XVIII–XIX, covering the intervening trials (being cast from a cliff, poisoned, bound and thrown into the sea), were not directly fetched in this batch and are therefore not quoted here, though referenced only in general terms via the app's existing figure summary.

documents.text: Ramakrishna was born in the village of Kamarpukar, in the Zillah Hugli, on the 20th of February, 1833. His father, Khudiram Chattopadhyaya, was the head of the only Brahmanic family in the village and, though very poor, 'would rather starve than stray from the strictest path of Brahmanical orthodoxy.' The name given to the child was Gadadhara, a name of Vishnu, given on account of a dream in which the deity told his father he would be born as his son; it was only later in life that he began to be called Ramakrishna.
documents.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

documents.text: When his elder brother fell ill, Ramakrishna took charge of worship at the temple of the goddess Kali at Dakshineswar, and 'began to look upon the image of the goddess Kali as his mother and the mother of the universe. He believed it to be living and breathing and taking food out of his hand.' After the regular forms of worship he would sit for hours, singing hymns and praying to her as a child to his mother, 'till he lost all consciousness of the outward world.'
documents.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

documents.text: Ramakrishna underwent 'twelve years of unheard-of tapasya, or ascetic exercises,' during which, he later recalled, 'a great religious tornado, as it were, raged within him.' He never once slept soundly through those years; he wept for hours calling out, 'Mother, oh my mother, another day has gone, and still I have not found thee,' and prayed, 'Mother! destroy in me all idea that I am great, and that I am a Brahman, and that they are low and pariahs, for who are they but Thou in so many forms?'
documents.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

documents.text: To teach his own soul detachment from wealth, Ramakrishna would sit by the Ganges with gold and silver coins in one hand and a handful of rubbish in the other, telling himself, 'this is what the world calls money... but it can never help thee to realise the ever-existent knowledge and bliss, the Brahman. Regard it, therefore, as rubbish,' before throwing both into the river. When a wealthy disciple once draped him in a costly gold-fringed shawl, he threw it to the ground and used it to clean the floor, saying it 'increases vanity, but it can never help to realise the ever-existent knowledge and bliss, and therefore is no better than a piece of torn rag.'
documents.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

documents.text: Of how seekers were drawn to him without his seeking fame, Ramakrishna himself observed: 'When the rose is blown, and sheds its fragrance all around, the bees come of themselves. The bees seek the full-blown rose, and not the rose the bees.' He came to teach that all religions are true, 'though each of them takes account of one aspect only' of the one undivided and eternal reality -- having in turn practiced Vaishnava devotion, Vedantic renunciation, and even, in his later years, Christian and Islamic contemplation, each time arriving quickly at what he held to be their common core.
documents.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

documents.text: In his final illness, from what began as 'the clergyman's throat' and developed into cancer, physicians advised Ramakrishna to keep strict silence, but he would not. Crowds gathered wherever he went and waited to hear a word from him, and 'he, out of compassion for them, would not remain silent,' saying, 'I would suffer willingly all sorts of bodily pains, and death also, a hundred thousand times, if by so doing I could bring one single soul to freedom and salvation.' He died on the night of 16 August 1886, passing into a samadhi from which, unlike his daily trances, he did not return.
documents.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)

documents.text: Ramakrishna felt such aversion to gold and silver that he could not touch them without physical distress, and he twice declined offers of a temple and a substantial yearly income, saying he would have to flee the place if the gift were pressed on him. Of himself he would say only that he was 'servant of all men and women,' looking on them all as God, and would touch the ground reverently where his own disciples had walked -- a humility his followers, including the young Narendranath Datta who became Swami Vivekananda, carried forward as the foundation of his teaching.
documents.source_name: Ramakrishna, His Life and Sayings, by F. Max Muller, 'Ramakrishna's Life' (London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1898)
