documents.text: After the fall of Jhansi and the defeat at Kalpi in May 1858, the Rani of Jhansi fled with Rao Sahib toward Gopalpur, where Tantia Topi joined them. Their affairs seemed desperate: they had lost central India, the Sagar and Narbada territories, and Bundelkhand, and enemy columns were closing in from every side.
documents.source_name: Colonel G. B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny of 1857-8, Vol. V (1897)

documents.text: Malleson records that of the confederate leaders, the Rani of Jhansi alone "possessed the genius, the daring, the despair necessary for the conception of great deeds," and that the desperate plan to march on and seize the fortress-city of Gwaliar from Maharajah Sindhia -- appealing to his troops' national feeling and turning it into a stronghold of resistance -- was almost certainly hers: "The conjecture, then, almost amounts to certainty that the desperate remedy... was suggested and pressed upon her comrades by the daring Rani of Jhansi."
documents.source_name: Colonel G. B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny of 1857-8, Vol. V (1897)

documents.text: After the plan succeeded and Gwaliar was taken, "the command of the bulk of the troops, encamped outside the city, was entrusted to the Rani of Jhansi." Malleson notes that no one, "not even Sir Hugh Rose, had imagined the height of daring to which the Rani of Jhansi would carry her audacious plans" -- so bold that the British at first believed the march on Gwaliar must be a trap rather than a genuine attempt to seize it.
documents.source_name: Colonel G. B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny of 1857-8, Vol. V (1897)

documents.text: At the Battle of Kotah-ki-Sarai (18 June 1858), "clad in the attire of a man and mounted on horseback, the Rani of Jhansi might have been seen animating her troops throughout the day." When the British 8th Hussars finally charged and broke the rebel line, she boldly fronted the British horsemen even as her own comrades gave way around her.
documents.source_name: Colonel G. B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny of 1857-8, Vol. V (1897)

documents.text: As she tried to escape with the others, her horse stumbled crossing a canal near the cantonment. "A hussar close upon her track, ignorant of her sex and her rank, cut her down. She fell to rise no more." Malleson records that that night her devoted followers, determined that the English should not boast of capturing her even dead, cremated her body themselves.
documents.source_name: Colonel G. B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny of 1857-8, Vol. V (1897)

documents.text: Malleson writes of the aftermath: "Though one bitter enemy, the Rani of Jhansi, had disappeared," the resistance in central India continued under Tantia Topi for months afterward -- a testament, in the historian's own framing, to how central her leadership and resolve had been to the wider 1857-58 uprising in the region.
documents.source_name: Colonel G. B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny of 1857-8, Vol. V (1897)

documents.text: Malleson, writing as a British military historian, nonetheless closes his account with a tribute: "Whatever her faults in British eyes may have been, her countrymen will ever believe that she was driven by ill-treatment into rebellion; that her cause was a righteous cause; and that the treatment she received at the hands of Lord Dalhousie was one of the main causes of the disaffection in Bundelkhand and Central India in 1857-8. To them she will always be a heroine."
documents.source_name: Colonel G. B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny of 1857-8, Vol. V (1897)

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Colonel G. B. Malleson's History of the Indian Mutiny of 1857-8, Vol. V (1897), Book 14, Chapter 3, 'Sir Hugh Rose and Gwaliar', as transcribed and hosted by the ibiblio.org 'British Raj' public-domain text collection. The work is a British colonial military history and its perspective should be read with that context in mind; it is used here as a documentary, contemporaneous, rights-clear primary source rather than a modern biography, per project sourcing policy.
documents.source_name: Colonel G. B. Malleson, History of the Indian Mutiny of 1857-8, Vol. V (1897)

documents.text: The Kalpa Sutra records that the Arhat Rishabha, the Kosalian, descended from heaven and took the form of an embryo in the womb of Marudevi, wife of the patriarch Nabhi, in Ikshvakubhumi. He belonged to the Kasyapa gotra, and had five names: Rishabha, First King, First Mendicant, First Jina, and First Tirthakara -- the first of the twenty-four Jinas whose lives the Kalpa Sutra records.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: As a king, Rishabha 'taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men' -- establishing, in Jain tradition, the arts and civilization by which humankind first learned to sustain itself.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: Having ruled for millions of years, Rishabha 'anointed his hundred sons as kings, and gave each a kingdom.' Then, riding to the park called Siddhartha Vana and the tree Asoka, 'after fasting two and a half days without drinking water, [he] put on a divine robe, and together with four thousand of high, noble, royal persons, and Kshatriyas, he tore out his hair, and leaving the house entered the state of houselessness' -- renouncing his entire kingdom and family at the height of his power.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: The Kalpa Sutra records that 'the Arhat Rishabha, the Kosalian, for one thousand years neglected his body' in ascetic practice, meditating upon himself for a thousand years before attaining omniscience -- the longest recorded austerity of any of the twenty-four Jinas in the text.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: Outside the town of Purimatala, under the tree Nyagrodha, 'after fasting three and a half days without drinking water, being engaged in deep meditation,' Rishabha 'reached the infinite... highest knowledge and intuition called Kevala' -- omniscience -- becoming, in Jain tradition, the first being of this era to attain full liberation-knowledge and to teach it to others.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: The Kalpa Sutra records that Rishabha had eighty-four Ganas and eighty-four Ganadharas (chief disciples), and 'an excellent community of eighty-four thousand Shramanas with Rishabhasena at their head,' three hundred thousand nuns led by Brahmisundari, over three hundred thousand lay votaries led by Sreyamsa, and over five hundred thousand female lay votaries led by Subhadra -- among the largest monastic communities recorded of any Tirthakara in the text.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

documents.text: On the summit of Mount Ashtapada, in the company of ten thousand monks, 'after fasting six and a half days without drinking water,' Rishabha died and attained final liberation. The Kalpa Sutra closes his account with the words: 'End of the Life of Rishabha. End of the Lives of the Ginas [Jinas]' -- marking him as the first and, in this text's arrangement, the culminating figure among the lives of the Tirthakaras it records.
documents.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

The Kalpa Sutra narrates Rishabha's life using the same formulaic template applied to Mahavira and the other Jinas in the same text; this manifest preserves that formal scriptural register rather than paraphrasing it into free narrative.

documents.text: Journeying east in search of Sita, Rama and Lakshman came to the hermitage of the aged ascetic woman Savari (Shabari), deep in the wood near Pampa. She rose to greet them with hands upraised, bowed low, washed their feet, and offered them water — a lifetime's devotion arriving, at last, at the moment she had waited for.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

documents.text: Shabari told Rama that her own teachers, great saints, had ascended to heaven from that very grove, but had left her a prophecy before they departed: 'In this pure grove, O devotee, Prince Rama soon will visit thee. When he and Lakshman seek this shade, be to thy guests all honour paid. Him shalt thou see, and pass away to those blest worlds which ne'er decay.' She had kept fruit gathered from every tree on Pampa's shore in store for this exact visit.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

documents.text: Rama addressed her first not with a demand but with concern for her spiritual well-being: 'I trust no cares invade thy peace, while holy works and zeal increase; that thou content with scanty food all touch of ire hast long subdued; that all thy vows are well maintained... that reverence of the saints who taught the faithful heart due fruit has brought.'
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

documents.text: Shabari answered that meeting Rama was itself the fruit of all her penance: 'My penance' meed this day I see complete, my lord, in meeting thee. This day the fruit of birth I gain, nor have I served the saints in vain... I feel, great lord, thy gentle eye my earthly spirit purify.' She then led the brothers through the grove, showing them the altars, lakes, and relics of the saints she had served for years.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

documents.text: Having completed her long vigil of waiting and service, Shabari asked Rama's leave to end her life and join her departed teachers: 'Permit thy servant, lord, I pray, to cast this mortal shell away, for I would dwell, this life resigned, with those great saints of lofty mind, whom I within this holy shade with reverential care obeyed.'
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

documents.text: Rama granted her wish simply and with respect: 'Go, lady, where thou fain wouldst be, O thou who well hast honoured me.' Shabari then resigned her body to flame and rose to heaven 'like the fire that burns and glows,' in celestial garments, 'bright with celestial gems,' attaining the sphere reserved for saints of the purest devotion.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

documents.text: Shabari's episode is treasured in the bhakti tradition as proof that devotion, patience, and simple hospitality — offered by someone with no scriptural learning or high birth, only unwavering faith — earns the same divine regard as the greatest penance. Her fruit, given with love, is remembered as more precious than any ritual offering.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Ralph T. H. Griffith's verse translation of the Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889, unambiguously public domain), Book III, Chapter LXXV ('Savari'), fetched directly from wisdomlib.org's hosting of this public-domain translation.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book III Chapter LXXV

documents.text: Shivaji's character was shaped by his mother Jijabai, who taught him stories of ancient heroes, and Dadoji Kondadev, who trained him in administration and military tactics in the rugged valleys of Maval.
documents.source_name: Shivaji and His Times, by Jadunath Sarkar (1919)

documents.text: Shivaji's goal was not merely personal kingdom but the establishment of a self-governing state where all people could practice their faith without fear of oppression, known as Hindavi Swarajya (self-rule).
documents.source_name: Shivaji and His Times, by Jadunath Sarkar (1919)

documents.text: When Adil Shahi general Afzal Khan marched with a massive army to crush the Marathas, Shivaji met him in a personal interview under Pratapgad, successfully defending himself and defeating the larger force through strategic foresight.
documents.source_name: Shivaji and His Times, by Jadunath Sarkar (1919)

documents.text: Imprisoned by Aurangzeb in Agra, Shivaji maintained his composure and escaped by concealing himself in large sweetmeat baskets, returning safely to Maharashtra to resume his struggle for independence.
documents.source_name: Shivaji and His Times, by Jadunath Sarkar (1919)

documents.text: Baji Prabhu Deshpande and a handful of soldiers held the pass of Ghodkhind (Pavankhind) to allow Shivaji to escape to Vishalgad, sacrificing their lives so their leader could survive to lead the Maratha cause.
documents.source_name: Shivaji and His Times, by Jadunath Sarkar (1919)

documents.text: Shivaji ordered his soldiers never to damage mosques, to treat women and children of all communities with respect, and to hand over any copy of the Quran found in battle to Muslim officers, instituting a model of religious tolerance.
documents.source_name: Shivaji and His Times, by Jadunath Sarkar (1919)

documents.text: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674, establishing a sovereign Hindu kingdom that could challenge imperial hegemony and preserve local culture, language, and traditions.
documents.source_name: Shivaji and His Times, by Jadunath Sarkar (1919)

documents.text: This entry compiles the historical records and translations from Jadunath Sarkar's "Shivaji and His Times" (1919), which is in the public domain.
documents.source_name: Shivaji and His Times, by Jadunath Sarkar (1919)

documents.text: Siddhartha Gautama left his palace, wife, and child to seek the end of suffering, wandering as an ascetic before achieving Enlightenment under the Bodhi tree and becoming the Buddha.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: Setting in motion the Wheel of Dharma (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) in his first sermon, the Buddha taught the Middle Way between self-indulgence and self-mortification, and the Four Noble Truths.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: Before his enlightenment, the Buddha practiced extreme fasting, eating only a single grain of rice a day, until he realized that physical torture does not lead to spiritual clarity.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: The Buddha calmly faced multiple attempts on his life by his cousin Devadatta, including a runaway wild elephant, which he tamed with loving-kindness.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: Even when mortally ill from his last meal, the Buddha walked long distances to Kusinara, instructing his disciples to not blame the donor of the food.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: "Therefore, O Ananda, be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves. Betake yourselves to no external refuge. Hold fast to the truth as a lamp." The Buddha emphasized personal realization.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" These were the last words of the Tathagata before he entered Parinirvana.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: This entry compiles the historical accounts and translations from T. W. Rhys Davids' "Buddhist Suttas" (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11, 1881), which is in the public domain and hosted on sacred-texts.com.
documents.source_name: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 11), translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1881)

documents.text: Earth herself, overburdened by the tyranny of demon-kings including Kansa of Mathura (a revival of the great Asura Kalanemi), went to the assembly of the gods on Mount Meru and pleaded for relief: 'Illustrious deities, do you so act that I may be relieved from my burden, lest helpless I sink into the nethermost abyss.'
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book V Chapters I & III

documents.text: Brahma led the gods to Vishnu on the milky sea and praised him at length before asking for aid. Vishnu answered by plucking two hairs, one white and one black, and declaring: 'This my (black) hair shall be impersonated in the eighth conception of the wife of Vasudeva, Devaki... and shall slay Kansa, who is the demon Kalanemi.'
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book V Chapters I & III

documents.text: Kansa, warned that Devaki's eighth child would be his death, had already imprisoned Vasudeva and Devaki and killed six of their infants as each was born, per Vasudeva's own promise made years earlier to spare Devaki's life at their wedding: 'Kill not Devaki, great warrior; spare her life, and I will deliver to you every child that she may bring forth.'
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book V Chapters I & III

documents.text: At Krishna's birth at midnight, 'the strong winds were hushed, and the rivers glided tranquilly... the gods, walking the sky, showered down flowers upon the earth.' Vasudeva, seeing his son's four-armed celestial form and the mark of Srivatsa on his breast, begged him to 'withhold this thy celestial form,' fearing Kansa would kill him the moment the child's nature was known.
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book V Chapters I & III

documents.text: That same night, with the guards charmed into sleep by Yoganidra, Vasudeva carried the infant out through a raging storm to exchange him for the newborn daughter of Yashoda in Gokula. Crossing the flooded Yamuna river with the child in his arms, 'the waters were stilled, and rose not above his knee,' while the great serpent Shesha spread his hoods overhead to shield them from the rain.
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book V Chapters I & III

documents.text: When Kansa learned of the birth and seized what he believed was Devaki's eighth child, he 'threw it ruthlessly against a stone' — but the infant (in truth Yashoda's daughter, the goddess Yoganidra) rose into the sky in gigantic eight-armed form and warned him: 'What avails it thee, Kansa, to have hurled me to the ground? he is born who shall kill thee... Now quickly secure him, and provide for thine own welfare.'
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book V Chapters I & III

documents.text: This exchange — Krishna smuggled to safety in Gokula while a goddess took his place to warn and torment Kansa — begins the entire cycle of Krishna's hidden childhood among the cowherds, his eventual return to Mathura, and Kansa's downfall, all framed by the Purana as Vishnu's direct incarnation 'for the sole object of maintaining piety in the world.'
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book V Chapters I & III

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Horace Hayman Wilson's 1840 translation of the Vishnu Purana (Wilson died 1860; translation unambiguously public domain), Book V, Chapters I ('The death of Kansa announced') and III ('Birth of Krishna'), fetched directly from sacred-texts.com's hosting of this public-domain translation. This batch covers only the birth and infant exchange; Krishna's childhood at Gokula (the butter-theft tales, Kaliya, Govardhana), his youth, and the Bhagavad Gita episode were not directly fetched/verified in this batch and are not represented.
documents.source_name: H. H. Wilson (trans.), The Vishnu Purana (1840), Book V Chapters I & III

documents.text: On the eve of his coronation, Rama came before his father King Dasaratha and found him sitting pale and speechless, unable to look at his son. When Rama pressed his stepmother Kaikeyi to explain, she answered without shame: the king had once granted her two boons, and she now claimed them — that her own son Bharat be crowned in Rama's place, and that Rama himself go into exile in the Dandak forest for fourteen years.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

documents.text: Rama's reply came without a flicker of grief: 'I, at the bidding of my sire, would cast my body to the fire, a deadly draught of poison drink, or in the waves of ocean sink: if he command, it shall be done, — my father and my king in one... It shall be done: let this suffice; Rama ne'er makes a promise twice.' He asked only why his father could not tell him this himself.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

documents.text: Rama accepted the sentence outright: 'Yea, for my father's promise sake I to the wood my way will take, and dwell a lonely exile there in hermit dress with matted hair... How can I fail his will to do, friend, master, grateful sovereign too?' He asked that messengers be sent at once to recall Bharat, so the kingdom would not lack a ruler for even a day.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

documents.text: When Kaikeyi, satisfied, urged him to leave the city immediately rather than wait for any formal ceremony, Rama answered with the principle that would define his life: 'I would not in this world remain a grovelling thrall to paltry gain, but duty's path would fain pursue, true as the saints themselves are true. From death itself I would not fly my father's wish to gratify... Amid all duties, Queen, I count this duty first and paramount, that sons, obedient, aye fulfil their honoured fathers' word and will.'
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

documents.text: Rama set aside every mark of royal rank without complaint — dismissing his chariot, his men, the chouries and white umbrella used for kings — and went to comfort his mother and gather Sita before departing. The text notes that though he had just lost an empire, 'the loss of empire could not dim the glory that encompassed him,' and that no citizen who saw him pass could read any change in his bearing.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

documents.text: Rama chose to conceal his own grief from the joyful crowds gathered for what they still believed was his coronation day: 'Thus to the palace Rama went where all were gay with hope and joy; but well he knew the dire event that hope would mar, that bliss destroy. So to his grief he would not yield lest the sad change their hearts might rend, and, the dread tiding unrevealed, spared from the blow each faithful friend.'
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

documents.text: Rama's exile — accepted instantly and without bitterness to preserve his father's word — becomes the founding act of the entire epic that follows: the fourteen years in the forest, the abduction of Sita, the war in Lanka, and eventually his restoration as king. The Ramayana holds up this single moment of unhesitating obedience to a father's promise as the model of dharma placed above personal claim to power.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Ralph T. H. Griffith's verse translation of the Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889; Griffith died 1906, translation unambiguously public domain), Book II, Chapters XVIII ('The Sentence') and XIX ('Rama's Promise'), fetched directly from wisdomlib.org's hosting of this public-domain translation. This batch covers only Rama's acceptance of exile; later books covering the war in Lanka and his return were not directly fetched/verified in this batch.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book II

documents.text: Describing his own search before he met his teacher, Vivekananda recalled: this man came to live near Calcutta, sending out sceptics by the hundreds every year, yet the great men from the different universities used to come and listen to him. 'I heard of this man, and I went to hear him. He looked just like an ordinary man, with nothing remarkable about him... and I thought, "Can this man be a great teacher?" I crept near to him and asked him the question which I had been asking others all my life: "Do you believe in God, Sir?"'
documents.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

documents.text: To his question the teacher, Sri Ramakrishna, answered simply, 'Yes.' 'Can you prove it, Sir?' 'Yes.' 'How?' 'Because I see Him just as I see you here, only in a much intenser sense.' Vivekananda recalled: 'That impressed me at once. For the first time I had found a man who dared to say that he saw God, that religion was a reality, to be felt, to be sensed...I began to come near that man, day after day, and I actually saw that religion could be given. One touch, one glance, can make a whole life change... when I myself saw this man, all scepticism was brushed aside.'
documents.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

documents.text: Of what he learned from his Master, Vivekananda taught: 'Religion is not talk, nor doctrines, nor theories, nor is it sectarianism. Religion cannot live in sects and societies. It is the relation between the soul and God... Religion does not consist in erecting temples, or building churches, or attending public worship. It is not to be found in books, nor in words, nor in lectures, nor in organizations. Religion consists in realization... The first ideal of this attempt to realize religion is that of renunciation.'
documents.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

documents.text: On the harmony of religions — the teaching that would carry him to the world stage at Chicago — Vivekananda said: 'The religions of the world are not contradictory nor antagonistic; they are but various phases of One Eternal Religion... we must respect all religions and we must try to accept them all as far as we can... "As different rivers, taking their start from different mountains, running crooked or straight, all come and mingle their waters in the ocean, so the different sects, with their different points of view, at last all come unto Thee."'
documents.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

documents.text: As Ramakrishna's fame drew ever larger crowds in his final illness, 'his intense love for mankind would not let him refuse to help even the humblest of the thousands who sought his aid,' though 'a vital throat disorder' had developed. Asked why he did not turn his own spiritual power to curing himself, he replied, 'My friend, I have thought you were a sage, but you talk like other men of the world. This mind has been given to the Lord, do you mean to say that I should take it back?' After his Master's death, Vivekananda and the other young disciples who carried on his work 'met with great antagonism, but they persevered' as wandering Sannyasins begging through the very streets where some had been born to first-class families.
documents.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

documents.text: In an address delivered to his countrymen during his return journey across India after the Parliament of Religions, Vivekananda called on them to reclaim their dignity: 'Oh India, forget not that your ideal woman is Sita, Savitri, Damayanti... forget not that from your very birth, you are sacrificed for the Mother... Hero, take courage, be proud that you are an Indian, — say, in pride, "I am an Indian, every Indian is my brother"... "the ignorant Indian, the poor Indian, the Brahman Indian, the Pariah Indian, is my brother."'
documents.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

documents.text: Vivekananda distilled his Master Sri Ramakrishna's message to the modern world in words that became the charter of his own life's work: 'Do not care for doctrines, do not care for dogmas, or sects, or churches or temples; they count for little compared with the essence of existence in each man which is spirituality... Earn that, first acquire that, and criticise no one, for all doctrines and creeds have some good in them... Be spiritual and realize truth for yourself.'
documents.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection (3rd revised ed., Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), an early compiled edition of Vivekananda's own lectures and addresses ('My Master' and his 1897 'Reply to Address of Welcome' tour speeches in India), fetched directly from the archive.org full-text scan (identifier speecheswritings00viveuoft). Vivekananda died in 1902 and his original lectures are unambiguously public domain; this specific early Natesan compilation is likewise in the public domain by age. The famous 1893 Chicago 'Sisters and Brothers of America' address itself was not directly fetched/verified within this batch and is therefore not quoted here.
documents.source_name: Speeches and Writings of Swami Vivekananda: A Comprehensive Collection, 3rd ed. (Madras: G. A. Natesan & Co.), 'My Master' and 'Reply to Address of Welcome'

documents.text: Reflecting on his own birth and early hardship, Tukaram sang: 'My mother grew weary of carrying me in the womb, so she delivered me; but she took no care that the spot was undefiled. She suffered agonies of heat and thirst and hunger -- why should she put me to her breast? The stake was on my own shoulders, I was on the road to death, yet even then I committed grievous crimes. Then, says Tuka, this was what happened to me: He touched me with his hand and set me behind his back.'
documents.source_name: The Poems of Tukarama, Vol. III, translated by J. Nelson Fraser (Madras: Christian Literature Society for India, 1915), 'Autobiography'

documents.text: Of the burdens of his householder life -- Tukaram was a shopkeeper by birth, weighed down by family and debt before his renunciation -- he sang: 'I have no use for thee now, O Shame! get hence, let me remember Rama. Through yielding to thee I ruined myself; I made myself the slave of this evil world... To gain pleasure I carried a wife on my shoulder; she brought a host of children upon me. I was taken before the four judges and the five; I was not suffered to entertain pure aspirations. Tuka says, Now I will drag thee across thorns; I have made God my champion.'
documents.source_name: The Poems of Tukarama, Vol. III, translated by J. Nelson Fraser (Madras: Christian Literature Society for India, 1915), 'Autobiography'

documents.text: Of his turn to Vithoba (Panduranga), the deity of Pandharpur to whom his life's devotion was given, Tukaram sang: 'I was caught by the press-gang as I stepped forward to meet the world, but on the way I met Vitthoba and he took compassion on me. I had a heavy load on my head, says Tuka; I was anxiously saying to myself, What generous man will meet me?'
documents.source_name: The Poems of Tukarama, Vol. III, translated by J. Nelson Fraser (Madras: Christian Literature Society for India, 1915), 'Autobiography'

documents.text: Of his renunciation of the world, Tukaram sang: 'I left the world on my own impulse; I was indeed heartily sick of it. Two things that are different cannot be forced to combine, just as buttermilk is for ever separate from butter. Both are produced by churning one substance, and different names are given to them... Tuka says, Where could a pearl ever find a dwelling place, if the mother-of-pearl were crushed?'
documents.source_name: The Poems of Tukarama, Vol. III, translated by J. Nelson Fraser (Madras: Christian Literature Society for India, 1915), 'Autobiography'

documents.text: On the means of crossing the sorrows of worldly life, Tukaram taught: 'So unfordable is the stream of life that we know not how to cross it. The savage beasts of lust and wrath fill us with dread. The eddies of illusion and desire whirl formidably round us. The billows of desire surge up; worldly transactions toss men to and fro. As the only means of passage, Tuka seats himself in the boat of the name' -- naming devout repetition of God's name as the vehicle of salvation open to all, regardless of learning or caste.
documents.source_name: The Poems of Tukarama, Vol. III, translated by J. Nelson Fraser (Madras: Christian Literature Society for India, 1915), 'Autobiography'

documents.text: Of surrendering his own will and standing apart from a hostile society -- Tukaram, a low-caste grocer by birth, faced real persecution from orthodox Brahmins for his popular devotional teaching -- he sang: 'This was the original step that averted my pangs; I presented my body at your feet; I was set free from toil and redeemed. Now I shall not suffer my own authority to guide me. Tuka stands apart from the world, far from all its worries.'
documents.source_name: The Poems of Tukarama, Vol. III, translated by J. Nelson Fraser (Madras: Christian Literature Society for India, 1915), 'Autobiography'

documents.text: On his own unworthiness redeemed by grace -- the humility that became central to his enduring reputation as a saint of the common people -- Tukaram sang: 'Should a jewel fall into the jaws of an alligator, a man of courage can pluck it forth with his hand; but the mind of a fool cannot be persuaded to the right path... If you rub sand very carefully you may perhaps extract divine oil from it. A hooded cobra provoked to fury you may perhaps hold in your hand like a flower. Lo! By the joy of Brahma, Tuka the greatest of sinners was saved.'
documents.source_name: The Poems of Tukarama, Vol. III, translated by J. Nelson Fraser (Madras: Christian Literature Society for India, 1915), 'Autobiography'

documents.text: This entry compiles verified passages from J. Nelson Fraser and K. B. Marathe's translation of Tukaram's abhangas, Volume III (Christian Literature Society for India, Madras, 1915), 'Autobiography' section (abhangas numbered by the Indo-Prakash edition, roughly 2649-2694), fetched directly from the archive.org full-text scan (identifier poemstukrma00maragoog). Tukaram died c. 1650 and this translation is unambiguously public domain by age. Because Tukaram is known chiefly through his own first-person songs rather than a separate biographical narrative, this manifest draws its narrative framing directly from those songs rather than from an external life account.
documents.source_name: The Poems of Tukarama, Vol. III, translated by J. Nelson Fraser (Madras: Christian Literature Society for India, 1915), 'Autobiography'

documents.text: Growse records that Tulsi Das was by descent a Brahman of the Kanaujiya clan. Tradition places his birth variously at Hastinapur or at Rajapur near Chitrakut. He studied for some length of time at Soron, and, as he himself records in the prologue to his Ramayana, commenced its composition at Ayodhya in the Sambat year 1631, corresponding to 1575 A.D. The greater part of his life was spent at Benares, though he also passed years in visits to Soron, Ayodhya, Chitrakut, Allahabad, and Brindaban. He died in the Sambat year 1680 (1624 A.D.).
documents.source_name: The Ramayana of Tulsi Das, translated by F. S. Growse, 'Introduction' (Allahabad, 1883)

documents.text: Tradition holds that Tulsi Das had great love for his wife; when she once went home to her father's without asking his leave, he forgot himself and hastened after her. Ashamed, she rebuked him in anger: 'Have you no love for Rama? My body is but a framework of skin and bone.' On hearing these words, Growse writes, 'it was, as it were, the daybreak; he felt compunction and left her and sped to the city of Kasi. There he made his abode, worshipping the lord publicly, making a rigid vow, and thirsting exceedingly for a vision.' Growse notes that, of all the traditional legends of the poet's life, this account of his wife first turning him from earthly to divine love 'may well be accepted as a fact.'
documents.source_name: The Ramayana of Tulsi Das, translated by F. S. Growse, 'Introduction' (Allahabad, 1883)

documents.text: According to the Bhakt-Mala's traditional account, a grateful spirit told Tulsi Das that a disguised Hanuman was always the first to arrive and the last to leave wherever the Ramayana was recited. Recognizing him as he left, Tulsi Das followed him into the wood and, knowing him to be the god, 'ran and embraced his feet, crying with a shout of joy: "You shall not escape me."' Perceiving his intense devotion, Hanuman assumed his famous form and asked what he wished; Tulsi Das answered, 'I am ever craving to behold with my very eyes the incomparable beauty of King Rama.' Hanuman told him where to meet him, and in time Rama and Lakshman appeared before him, mounted on horseback in green raiment like huntsmen.
documents.source_name: The Ramayana of Tulsi Das, translated by F. S. Growse, 'Introduction' (Allahabad, 1883)

documents.text: H. H. Wilson's account, drawn from the Bhakt-Mala, records that Tulsi Das's fame reached Delhi, where Shah Jahan was emperor. 'The monarch sent for him to produce the person of Rama, which Tulsi Das refusing to do, the king threw him into confinement.' Growse's fuller version has Tulsi Das answer the emperor's demand for a miracle plainly: 'It is false; know that Rama is all in all.' Thrown into prison for his refusal, 'thousands upon thousands of sturdy monkeys spread all over the place,' besieging the fort until the emperor, overwhelmed, ordered him freed and abandoned the site -- founding, in Wilson's telling, the new city of Shahjahanabad in its place.
documents.source_name: The Ramayana of Tulsi Das, translated by F. S. Growse, 'Introduction' (Allahabad, 1883)

documents.text: When a Brahman who had committed murder came on pilgrimage crying, 'For the love of Rama give an alms even to me, a murderer,' Tulsi Das received him, fed him from the god's own offerings, and 'purified him and sang the praises of his Beloved.' Challenged by other Brahmans for eating with a murderer, he answered, 'Read your books; their real meaning has not penetrated your heart; therefore your faith is dead and your blindness has not been removed' -- teaching that the repetition of the holy name of Rama redeems even the gravest sin, regardless of birth or caste.
documents.source_name: The Ramayana of Tulsi Das, translated by F. S. Growse, 'Introduction' (Allahabad, 1883)

documents.text: Growse records that Tulsi Das himself founded the temple of Sita-Ram at Benares, where an autograph manuscript of his minor work the Ram Agya was preserved until it was lost in the Mutiny. In addition to his great Ramayana, he composed at least six other poems -- the Ramgitavali, the Dohavali, the Kabit-sambandh, the Binay Patrika, the Satsai, and the Ram Agya -- 'all of them having the one object of popularizing the cultus of his tutelary divinity.'
documents.source_name: The Ramayana of Tulsi Das, translated by F. S. Growse, 'Introduction' (Allahabad, 1883)

documents.text: The Bhakt-Mala of Nabha Ji, one of the earliest notices of Tulsi Das, declares in Growse's translation: 'For the redemption of mankind in this perverse Kali Yug, Valmiki has been born again as Tulsi... Now again, as a blessing to the faithful, has he taken birth and published the sportive actions of the god. Intoxicated with his passion for Rama's feet, he perseveres day and night in the accomplishment of his vow, and has supplied, as it were, a boat for the easy passage of the boundless ocean of existence.'
documents.source_name: The Ramayana of Tulsi Das, translated by F. S. Growse, 'Introduction' (Allahabad, 1883)

Growse's Introduction to his 1883 English translation of the Ramcharitmanas, 'The Ramayana of Tulsi Das,' fetched directly from the archive.org full-text scan (identifier rmyanaoftuls00tulauoft). The Introduction itself quotes and translates the Bhakt-Mala (with Priya Das's 1713 Hindi gloss) and H. H. Wilson's 1828 'Essay on the Religious Sects of the Hindus.' Growse explicitly distinguishes the more reliably attested biographical facts (birth traditions, dates, works) from the traditional miracle legends, a distinction preserved in this manifest's framing. The translated epic text of the Ramcharitmanas itself was not fetched in this batch; only the biographical Introduction was used.

documents.text: After the sage Narada had told him the full story of Rama, Valmiki went to bathe in the river Tamasa with his pupil Bharadvaja, marvelling at the clear, pebbled shallow: 'clear as good men's bosoms are.'
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

documents.text: As Valmiki watched, an outcast fowler shot and killed the male of a pair of curlews sporting fearlessly by the bank; the hen bird shrieked in grief over her mate. Moved to sorrow and anger at the cruelty, Valmiki's heart 'with ruth was stirred,' and he pronounced a curse on the fowler in a rhythm he had never spoken before.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

documents.text: Valmiki realized, on reflection, that the words of grief he had cried out had come in perfectly balanced, measured lines — the world's first shloka. He named the new verse-form for the grief (shoka) that had produced it: 'With equal lines of even feet, with rhythm and time and tone complete, the measured form of words I spoke in shock of grief be termed a shloke.'
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

documents.text: That same day, Brahma the Creator himself appeared at Valmiki's hermitage. The sage rose in wondering awe, offered him water and a seat, yet found his mind still returning, unbidden, to the slain curlew — and the verse of grief kept forming on his lips even in the presence of the god.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

documents.text: Brahma smiled and told Valmiki the verse he had spoken unconsciously was itself the sign: 'A verse, unconscious thou hast made; no longer be the task delayed... The tuneful lines thy lips rehearsed spontaneous from thy bosom burst.' He then commissioned Valmiki directly to compose the entire life of Rama in this new verse form, promising: 'In all thy poem, through my grace, no word of falsehood shall have place.'
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

documents.text: Brahma's charge to Valmiki closed with a promise of the epic's endurance: 'As long as in this firm-set land the streams shall flow, the mountains stand, so long throughout the world, be sure, the great Ramayan shall endure... To higher spheres shalt thou arise and dwell with me above the skies!' He then vanished, leaving Valmiki to begin the work.
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

documents.text: Valmiki's own pupils, moved by love of their teacher, took up chanting the verse he had spoken by the river, marvelling at its balanced rhythm — and this became the metre in which Valmiki went on to compose 'hundreds of such verses, sweet with equal lines and even feet,' telling 'the glorious deeds of Rama' in what tradition reveres as the first work of poetry (Adi Kavya), with Valmiki honoured as the first poet (Adi Kavi).
documents.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

documents.text: Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsiang) was born in A.D. 603 at Ch'in Liu in the province of Ho-nan, the youngest of four brothers. Taken as a boy by his second brother, a monk, to the eastern capital Lo-yang, he was ordained at the Tsing-tu temple at the age of thirteen. Amid the troubles at the end of the Sui dynasty he fled with his brother to Shu-chu, capital of Sz'chuen, where at the age of twenty he was fully ordained as a Bhikshu.
documents.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

documents.text: Travelling through the provinces in search of the best instructors he could find, Xuanzang came at length to Chang'an. There, stirred by the memory of the earlier pilgrims Fa-hian and Chi-yen, he resolved, at twenty-six years of age, to journey to the western regions to question the sages on points that troubled his mind — setting out from Chang'an in the company of a fellow priest.
documents.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

documents.text: At Liang-chau, the entrepot for merchants from Tibet and beyond the Tsung-ling mountains, Xuanzang explained the sacred books and revealed his purpose of travelling to the kingdom of the Brahmans to seek the Law. Provided with means for his journey by grateful merchants, and 'notwithstanding the expostulation of the governor of the city,' he was able, through the connivance of two priests, to press onward westward as far as Kwa-chau — defying official efforts to stop him.
documents.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

documents.text: Going north with a young guide who had offered to lead him, Xuanzang crossed a river by night and, after escaping the treachery of that very guide, came on alone to the first of five watch-towers stretching toward the country of I-gu (Kamul), spaced at intervals of a hundred li. The text notes, without needing to recount every detail, 'the fervent prayers to Kwan-yin and his incessant invocation of the name of this divinity' by which the lone pilgrim sustained himself through the crossing.
documents.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

documents.text: Having prevailed on the keepers of the first and fourth watch-towers to let him pass, Xuanzang at last reached the confines of I-gu and halted there — only to be summoned by the prince of Kao-chang (Turfan), who attempted in vain to keep the pilgrim in his territory before finally releasing him onward toward 'O-ki-ni (Karasharh) and the long road to India via Kuche, the Icy Mountains, and the valley of the Chu river.
documents.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

documents.text: Xuanzang had been away from China since A.D. 629; he returned in A.D. 645, having crossed the Pamir and passed back through Kashgar and Khotan. He brought with him five hundred grains of relics of the Buddha's body, seven statues of the Buddha in gold, silver, and sandalwood, one hundred and twenty-four works of the Great Vehicle, and other texts amounting to 520 fascicles — carried, the record notes, by twenty-two horses.
documents.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang

documents.text: Of the many books Xuanzang translated after his return, seventy-five still survive within the collection of the Chinese Tripitaka. His travel record, the Si-Yu-Ki, together with the biography written by his disciple Hwui-lih, preserved for posterity a first-hand account of Buddhist India in the seventh century that remains a primary historical source to this day.
documents.source_name: Samuel Beal (trans.), Si-Yu-Ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Introduction (d): Hiuen Tsiang or Xuanzang
